note: Written to be spoken: one idea per line; {"beat": s} is a deliberate pause; numbers are phrased the way they are said, never as digits. Tool and flag names are spoken as their job, not their symbol. `answer` plays after the learner answers a predict step. Opens on the chapter bridge line and closes on the handoff line.

lines: Grouping events into episodes answered what happened.
Now: smoother statistics over the numbers themselves, running and moving, instead of just marking where one episode ends and the next begins.
A total that only ever grows is cheap to keep. Add the new number, move on.
A total over a sliding stretch... the last so many, nothing older... has to drop old numbers out just as often as it adds new ones in.
Same idea, total so far, but one of them has to remember how to let go, and that costs more.
Now, a trap that looks harmless.
Say you want last week's revenue, and you grab it by counting back a fixed number of rows.
On a day with twice the normal number of orders... does counting back that same fixed number of rows still cover a full week?
answer: No. It covers less time than usual, because more orders landed in the same stretch of rows.
Counting rows measures rows. It was never measuring days.
If you actually mean a week, you have to ask for a week, measured in time itself, not in how many rows happened to show up.

lines: Two more useful numbers, and they answer slightly different questions.
Ask for the middle value of a whole set, and one version will happily hand you a number that never actually appeared anywhere in your data... it just split the difference between two real values.
The other version refuses to invent anything. It always hands you back a value that was genuinely there.
Neither is wrong. One promises a smooth estimate. The other promises a real, traceable row. Pick the one your situation actually needs.
And one more worth knowing: splitting a whole group into even buckets... deciles, quartiles, whatever size you ask for... with no manual boundary math at all.
Here's the catch behind all of this.
A running total can be kept cheaply, one new number at a time, forever.
Can the middle value, or the ninety-ninth percentile, be kept just as cheaply, the same running way?
answer: The middle value of everything so far can shift because of any single new number, anywhere in the pile... not just the newest one.
So getting it exactly right means holding onto the whole ordered pile, every time.
At real scale, that's expensive enough that people often trade a little exactness away for a much cheaper estimate instead... a trade worth making on purpose, not by accident.

lines: So: a growing total is cheap, a sliding one costs a bit more, and both are still just totals.
A real week means time, not a row count.
And the middle of a pile, exactly, needs the whole pile in hand... which is exactly why people start trading exactness for speed, on purpose.
Comparing a row to its own neighbors is one kind of question.
Next: comparing a row to the exact value another table held, at that very moment in time.
